title: Shorter sliding windows (S = seq//4) on the r1 config
description: short_window = sequence_len//2 -> //4 (1024 -> 512) in GPT._compute_window_sizes, stacked on the round-1 replicated config (HEAD_DIM 64, TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE 2**18, DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE 128).
reflection:
val_bpb 0.989981 at queued_s=0 (cold card), 486.3M tokens, 1855 steps, MFU 35.86%, 45.0GB. Best number in the cell and the first one that beats the 0.992664 cold-card baseline on like-for-like terms: the matched cold-card control is r01/a0_v1 (same queue position, 474.5M tokens, 0.993168), so the delta is -0.0032 at sd ~0.0006.

The gain is NOT mostly throughput, and my own proposal was wrong about that. estimate_flops fell 239M -> 220.2M per token as predicted (-7.9%), but tokens only went 474.5M -> 486.3M (+2.5%), not the +8% I forecast, and MFU dropped 37.8% -> 35.86%. FA3 at window 512 is less efficient per FLOP than at 1024, so roughly two thirds of the arithmetic saving was eaten by the kernel. Correcting for the tokens actually gained (within-cluster slope -0.000128 bpb/1M), the token model predicts 0.9917; I measured 0.989981, i.e. ~-0.0017 of genuine quality improvement on top of the tokens.

So the mechanism is the one I argued as a side benefit, not the one I led with: prepare.py best-fit-packs several documents into each 2048-token row and fa3.flash_attn_func gets no document block mask, so attention span beyond a few hundred tokens is largely spent on unrelated documents. Narrowing the local window removes cross-document contamination. That reading predicts the next probe should be narrower still (seq//8 = 256) or a pattern with fewer full-attention layers, and it predicts the opposite direction (SSLL, all-long) will lose. It also suggests the largest remaining win on this axis is a real document mask, which is a bigger code change but attacks the cause directly.
